title: Mandodari's lament
hookLine: Ravana's queen walks onto the battlefield, and says what no one else could say
carry: mastering the senses is never done once

cards: When the noise of victory dies down, the gates of Lanka open, and the women of Ravana's palace come out onto the battlefield. They've lost husbands, sons, brothers. They walk among the dead, weeping, until they find him.
One of them comes forward and kneels by the body. She is Mandodari, Ravana's chief queen, Indrajit's mother. She has lost her son, and now her husband.
Valmiki lets her speak over him at length.

teach.b: Her lament holds love and truth at the same time. She remembers who he was. You frightened the gods, she says; the earth and the mountains trembled at your name.
How could a man on foot, wandering in the forest, bring you down?

teach.h: RAMA IS MORE THAN A MAN.
teach.b: First she answers that Rama can't be only a man; he must be Vishnu himself, come in human form. A queen of Lanka says it out loud, over her husband's body. Then she names Ravana's own part, gently and without flinching.
Long ago, she says, you conquered your senses, and with that discipline you conquered the three worlds.
Now it's as if your senses remembered, and took their revenge. Your desire for Sita did what no army could. This is one of Hinduism's most repeated teachings.

The Upanishads picture the senses, the indriyas, as strong horses pulling the chariot of the body, and the Bhagavad Gita warns that the restless senses can carry off the mind even of a wise person who is striving.

Mastery isn't won once and kept. It's one reason many Hindus keep vrats, small fasts and vows, again and again: practice in holding the reins. Ravana's tapas was legendary, and he stopped holding them.
Then Mandodari simply grieves: her husband, her son, her life in pieces.
Later tradition honored her among the five women, the panchakanya, whose remembrance is said to wash away wrongdoing. She saw him whole, and mourned him anyway.

how: Some Hindus recite a traditional verse naming five revered women of the epics, the pañcakanyā, with Mandodari among them, and some say it in the morning; versions differ on one of the names.

o: a dancer of Ravana's court who flees the city
Ravana's chief queen, who mourns him and names his fault
a queen of Ayodhya who waits for Rama's return

p: a small vow of holding back

s: Mandodari curses Rama over Ravana's body
she says Rama must be more than a man, and names Ravana's own fault.
she says Ravana once conquered his senses
and that his desire for Sita was their revenge.
once you've mastered your senses, you never have to again
Ravana once had; the Gita warns the senses can carry off even a wise mind.

games.q: a friend says: "Ravana did huge tapas, so desire couldn't touch him anymore." what fits Mandodari's lament?
o: no: even he had to keep holding the reins, and he let go.
desire doesn't matter if you're powerful enough.
games.why: Mandodari says he conquered his senses long ago, and his desire for Sita was their revenge. mastery is kept, not won once.

practice: Many Hindus keep a vrat, a small vow of holding back, on a set day. Try a tiny one now: choose one thing you'll go without today, a snack, a scroll, a second helping.
If you pray, offer it to God; if you don't, just notice the pull when it comes, and hold the reins for one breath longer.

wordCard.voice: Mandodari. Ravana's chief queen and Indrajit's mother, who grieves him on the battlefield, naming both his greatness and the senses that took their revenge.

orig.note: Sanskrit indriya: a sense, a sense power; the Upanishads picture the indriyas as horses, and the Gita warns they can carry off the mind.

carryVoice: Your line: mastering the senses is never done once. The king still lies on the field, waiting for his last rites. See you then.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda 110–111 (the women of Lanka come out; Mandodari's lament)

Bhagavad Gita 2.60 (the restless senses carry off the mind even of a wise person who strives)
Katha Upanishad 1.3.3–4 (the chariot image: the senses are the horses)
